title: Chapter XXXIII
paragraphs: The next day, Tuesday, Earnshaw was still unable to return to his usual work and remained around the house. I soon discovered that keeping my charge beside me as before was now impossible. She went downstairs ahead of me and out into the garden, where she had seen her cousin doing some light work. When I went to call them to breakfast, I found she had persuaded him to clear a large patch of currant and gooseberry bushes. They were busy planning which plants to bring over from the Grange.
The destruction they had managed in a mere half-hour horrified me. Those blackcurrant bushes were Joseph’s pride and joy, and she had chosen the very middle of them for a flower bed.

“There! The master will hear about all this the moment it’s discovered,” I exclaimed. “What excuse can you offer for taking such liberties with the garden? There’ll be a fine explosion over it, just you wait! Mr. Hareton, I’m surprised you haven’t more sense than to make such a mess at her bidding!”
“I forgot they were Joseph’s,” Earnshaw answered, looking rather disconcerted. “But I’ll tell him I did it.”

We always ate with Mr. Heathcliff. I performed the mistress’s duties of making tea and carving, so I was needed at the table. Catherine usually sat beside me, but that morning she edged closer to Hareton. I soon saw that she would be no more discreet in friendship than she had been in hostility.
“Mind you don’t talk to your cousin too much or pay him too much attention,” I whispered as we entered. “It will certainly annoy Mr. Heathcliff, and he’ll be angry with both of you.”
“I won’t,” she answered.
A minute later she had sidled up to Hareton and was putting primroses in his porridge.

He dared not speak to her there, scarcely even look at her. Yet she kept teasing until twice she almost made him laugh. I frowned, and she glanced towards the master, whose face showed that his mind was occupied with something quite apart from his companions. For a moment she grew serious and studied him intently. Then she turned back to her nonsense, until at last Hareton gave a stifled laugh. Mr. Heathcliff started and looked quickly from face to face. Catherine met his eyes with that mixture of nervousness and defiance which he hated.

“It’s just as well you’re out of my reach!” he exclaimed. “What devil possesses you to keep staring back at me with those infernal eyes? Lower them! Don’t remind me you’re here again. I thought I’d cured you of laughing.”
“It was me,” Hareton muttered.
“What did you say?” the master demanded.

Hareton looked down at his plate and did not repeat his confession. Mr. Heathcliff watched him a moment, then silently returned to his breakfast and his interrupted thoughts. We had almost finished. The two young people wisely moved farther apart, and I expected no more trouble during the meal. Then Joseph appeared in the doorway. His trembling lip and furious eyes showed that he had discovered the outrage against his precious bushes. He must have seen Cathy and her cousin there before inspecting the damage. His jaws worked like a cow chewing its cud, making his words difficult to understand as he began:

“I must have my wages, and I must go! I’d _meant_ to die where I’ve served for sixty years. I thought I’d carry my books and all my bits o’ things up to t’ attic and let them have t’ kitchen to themselves, for peace’s sake. It was hard to give up my own hearth, but I thought I _could_ do that! Now she’s taken my garden, and by my heart, master, I can’t stand it! Thou can bend to t’ yoke if thou likes. I’m not used to it, and an old man doesn’t soon take to new burdens. I’d sooner earn my bread and drink breaking stones on t’ road!”
“Now, now, you idiot!” Heathcliff interrupted. “Make it short! What’s your grievance? I won’t interfere in quarrels between you and Nelly. She can shut you in the coal cellar for all I care.”

“It’s not Nelly!” Joseph answered. “I wouldn’t leave for Nelly, nasty good-for-nowt though she is. Thank God! _she_ can’t steal anybody’s soul! She’s never been so handsome a body couldn’t look at her without blinking. It’s yon dreadful, graceless hussy who’s bewitched our lad with her bold eyes and forward ways, till—Nay! It fair breaks my heart! He’s forgotten all I’ve done for him, all I’ve made of him, and gone and torn up a whole row of t’ finest currant bushes in t’ garden!” At that he broke into open lamentation, overcome by the bitterness of his injuries and by Earnshaw’s ingratitude and dangerous state.
“Is the fool drunk?” Mr. Heathcliff asked. “Hareton, is it you he’s complaining about?”
“I’ve pulled up two or three bushes,” the young man replied, “but I’ll plant them again.”
“Why did you pull them up?” the master asked.
Catherine thought it wise to put in a word.
“We wanted to plant flowers there,” she cried. “It’s entirely my fault. I asked him to do it.”
“And who the devil gave _you_ permission to touch a stick in this place?” her father-in-law demanded, much astonished. Turning to Hareton, he added, “And who told _you_ to obey her?”
Hareton could not speak. His cousin answered, “You shouldn’t begrudge me a few yards of earth to make pretty when you’ve taken all my land!”
“Your land, you insolent slut! You never had any,” Heathcliff said.
“And my money,” she went on, returning his angry stare while biting the last crust of her breakfast.
“Silence!” he cried. “Finish and get out!”
“And Hareton’s land and money,” the reckless girl continued. “Hareton and I are friends now, and I’m going to tell him everything about you!”
For a moment the master seemed stunned. He went pale and stood, never taking his eyes from her, with a look of deadly hatred.
“If you hit me, Hareton will hit you,” she said. “So you might as well sit down.”

“If Hareton doesn’t throw you out, I’ll knock him straight to hell!” Heathcliff thundered. “Damned witch! Do you dare try to turn him against me? Get her out! Do you hear? Throw her into the kitchen! Ellen Dean, if you let her come in my sight again, I’ll kill her!”
Under his breath, Hareton tried to persuade her to leave.
“Drag her away!” Heathcliff shouted savagely. “Are you standing there talking?” He came forward to carry out the order himself.
“He won’t obey you any more, you wicked man,” Catherine said. “And soon he’ll hate you as much as I do.”
“Hush! Hush!” the young man muttered reproachfully. “I won’t hear thee speak to him like that. Stop it.”
“But you won’t let him hit me?” she cried.
“Then come away,” he whispered urgently.
It was too late. Heathcliff had seized her.
“Now _you_ go!” he told Earnshaw. “Accursed witch! This time she’s provoked me when I couldn’t bear it. I’ll make her regret it for the rest of her life!”

His hand was tangled in her hair. Hareton tried to loosen his grip, begging him not to hurt her this once. Heathcliff’s dark eyes blazed. He looked ready to tear Catherine apart, and I had just worked myself up to risk rescuing her when suddenly his fingers loosened. He moved his grip from her hair to her arm and stared intently into her face. Then he passed a hand over his eyes and stood a moment, apparently collecting himself. Turning back to Catherine, he said with forced calm, “You must learn not to drive me into a rage, or one day I really will murder you! Go with Mrs. Dean and stay with her. Let her be the only one who hears your insolence. As for Hareton Earnshaw, if I see him listening to you, I’ll send him out to find his bread where he can get it! Your love will make him an outcast and a beggar. Nelly, take her away. Leave me, all of you! Leave me!”

I led my young mistress out. She was too glad to escape to resist. Hareton followed, leaving Mr. Heathcliff alone until dinner. I had advised Catherine to eat upstairs, but when he saw her empty place he sent me to fetch her. He spoke to none of us, ate very little, and went out directly afterwards, saying he would not return until evening.

While he was away, the two new friends settled in the main room. There I heard Hareton sharply stop his cousin when she offered to explain how her father-in-law had treated his father. He would not allow a word against him, he said. Even if Heathcliff were the devil, it made no difference: he would stand by him. He would rather she abused him as she used to than attack Mr. Heathcliff. Catherine was growing angry, but he found a way to silence her by asking how she would like _him_ to speak badly of her father. Then she understood that Earnshaw felt the master’s reputation as his own, and was attached to him by bonds stronger than reason could break—chains forged by habit, which it would be cruel to try to loosen. Afterwards she showed her good heart by avoiding both complaints about Heathcliff and expressions of hatred. She told me she was sorry she had tried to set him and Hareton against each other. Indeed, I don’t believe she has spoken a single word against her oppressor in Hareton’s hearing since.

Once this small disagreement ended, they were friends again and completely absorbed in their roles of pupil and teacher. When my work was done, I went to sit with them. Watching them gave me such peace and comfort that I lost all sense of time. You see, I felt they were both my children in a way. I had long been proud of one, and now I was sure the other would make me just as happy. His honest, warm, intelligent nature was rapidly shaking off the ignorance and degradation in which it had been raised. Catherine’s genuine praise drove him to work harder. As his mind brightened, so did his face, gaining life and dignity. I could scarcely believe he was the same person I had seen when I found my little mistress at Wuthering Heights after her expedition to the Crags. While I watched with admiration and they worked, dusk fell, and the master returned. He came upon us quite unexpectedly through the front door and saw all three of us before we could raise our heads. Well, I thought, there could be no pleasanter or more innocent sight. Scolding them would be shameful. The red firelight shone on their two lovely heads and showed their faces alive with the eager interest of children. Though he was twenty-three and she eighteen, both had so much new to feel and learn that neither felt or displayed the sobriety of disenchanted adulthood.

They looked up together at Mr. Heathcliff. Perhaps you have never noticed that their eyes are exactly alike, and that they are Catherine Earnshaw’s eyes. The younger Catherine has no other resemblance to her, apart from a broad forehead and a certain curve of the nostril that makes her look rather proud whether she means to or not. In Hareton the resemblance goes further. It is remarkable at any time, but _then_ it was especially striking, because his senses were keen and his mind was unusually awake and active. I suppose that likeness disarmed Mr. Heathcliff. He walked towards the hearth, visibly agitated, but the agitation quickly subsided as he looked at the young man—or rather changed its character, for it was still there. He took the book from Hareton’s hand, glanced at the open page, and returned it without comment. He merely motioned Catherine away. Her companion followed almost immediately. I too was about to go, but he told me to stay seated.

“A poor ending, isn’t it?” he said, after dwelling for a while on what he had just seen. “An absurd conclusion to all my violent efforts? I gather levers and pickaxes to demolish both houses. I train myself to work like Hercules. Then, when everything is ready and within my power, I find I haven’t the will to lift one slate from either roof! My old enemies haven’t beaten me. Now would be exactly the time to revenge myself on those who stand in their place. I could do it, and no one could stop me. But what’s the point? I no longer care to strike. I can’t be bothered to raise my hand! That makes it sound as though I’ve worked all this time merely to display some splendid generosity. Nothing could be further from the truth. I’ve lost the ability to enjoy their destruction, and I’m too idle to destroy them for nothing.

“Nelly, a strange change is coming. I’m in its shadow now. My daily life interests me so little that I hardly remember to eat or drink. Those two who just left are the only things that still seem solid and distinct to me, and the sight of them hurts almost beyond endurance. I won’t speak about _her_, and I don’t want to think about her. I earnestly wish she were invisible: her presence rouses nothing but feelings that drive me mad. _He_ affects me differently. Yet if I could avoid ever seeing him again without appearing insane, I would! Perhaps you’ll think I’m heading that way,” he added, trying to smile, “if I describe the thousand memories and ideas he awakens or embodies. But you won’t repeat what I tell you. My mind has been shut up inside itself so endlessly that at last it’s tempting to open it to someone else.

“Five minutes ago Hareton seemed the embodiment of my youth, not a human being. I felt so many different things towards him that I couldn’t possibly have spoken to him rationally. First, his astonishing likeness to Catherine bound him to her in a terrible way. You might think that was what most powerfully seized my imagination, but it is actually the least of it. What _isn’t_ connected with her for me? What doesn’t remind me of her? I can’t look at this floor without seeing her features formed in the flagstones! In every cloud and every tree, filling the air at night and glimpsed in every object by day, her image surrounds me! The most ordinary faces of men and women—even my own face—mock me with a resemblance. The whole world is a dreadful collection of reminders that she existed and I have lost her! Well, in Hareton’s face I saw the ghost of my undying love, my wild struggles to hold on to what was mine, my degradation, my pride, my happiness, my anguish—

“But it’s madness to repeat these thoughts to you. It only explains why, though I dislike always being alone, his company does me no good. It worsens the constant torment I live with. That’s partly why I no longer care how he and his cousin get on together. I can’t pay them any more attention.”

“But what do you mean by a _change_, Mr. Heathcliff?” I asked, alarmed by his manner. In my judgment, however, he was neither about to lose his mind nor to die. He was perfectly strong and healthy. As for his sanity, he had taken pleasure since childhood in brooding over dark things and entertaining strange fancies. He might have an obsessive madness concerning the idol he had lost, but on every other subject his mind was as sound as mine.
“I won’t know until it comes,” he said. “I’m only half aware of it now.”
“You don’t feel ill, do you?” I asked.
“No, Nelly, I don’t,” he answered.
“Then you’re not afraid of dying?” I continued.

“Afraid? No!” he replied. “I neither fear death nor foresee it nor hope for it. Why should I? With my strong constitution, moderate habits, and harmless occupations, I ought to remain above ground until there’s hardly a black hair left on my head, and probably _will_. Yet I can’t go on like this! I have to remind myself to breathe, almost remind my heart to beat! It’s like forcing back a stiff spring. I must compel myself to make the slightest movement that doesn’t spring from one thought, or to notice anything, living or dead, unconnected with that one all-embracing idea. I have a single wish. My entire being, all my powers, yearn to fulfil it. They’ve yearned for it so long and so steadily that I’m certain it _will_ be fulfilled, and _soon_, because it has consumed my life. I’m swallowed up in anticipating it. Confessing hasn’t relieved me, but perhaps it explains some otherwise inexplicable moods of mine. O God! It’s a long struggle. I wish it were over!”

He began pacing the room and muttering dreadful things to himself. I was almost persuaded, as he said Joseph had been, that his conscience had turned his heart into a hell on earth. I wondered greatly how it would end. Though he had seldom revealed this state of mind before, even in his expression, I had no doubt it was his usual condition. He said so himself. Yet no one could have guessed it from his ordinary behaviour. You didn’t, Mr. Lockwood, when you met him. At the time I’m describing he was just as he was then, only more inclined to long periods alone and perhaps even less talkative in company.
